summary: The Compression ratio calculator turns the head gasket thickness, the deck clearance and more into compression ratio. It suits a practical question that turns up in daily life. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Compression ratio calculator work?
sections.html:
The Compression ratio calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports compression ratio in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the head gasket thickness (t), the deck clearance (c), the combustion chamber volume and the piston volume.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Compression ratio calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Compression ratio=(compressed volume + displacement volume) ÷ compressed volume
Gasket volume=-combustion chamber volume − clearance volume − displacement volume − piston volume + swept volume
Compressed volume=combustion chamber volume + clearance volume + gasket volume + piston volume
Displacement volume=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × (bore diameter (b) ^ 2) × piston stroke (s)
Gasket volume=(1 ÷ 4) × PI × head gasket thickness (t) × (gasket bore (g) ^ 2)
Bore diameter (b)=2 × the square root of (clearance volume ÷ deck clearance (c)) ÷ the square root of (PI)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Number of cylinders = 1, Head gasket thickness (t) = 0.09 mm, Deck clearance (c) = 0 mm and Piston volume = 0 cc. Working through the relationship above gives Engine volume = 10 cc and Compression ratio = 2.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Engine volume = 10 cc and Compression ratio = 2 should be roughly the size you expected from Number of cylinders = 1 and Head gasket thickness (t) = 0.09 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Compression ratio calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the head gasket thickness, the deck clearance and the combustion chamber volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Compression ratio calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns compression ratio, derived from the head gasket thickness, the deck clearance and the combustion chamber volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Compression ratio calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the head gasket thickness, the deck clearance, the combustion chamber volume and the piston volume, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter bore diameter (b) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Bore diameter (b) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Engine volume = 10 cc. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Compression ratio calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
